steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on reinforcement learning for freeform robot design, where a policy-gradient method builds robots out of voxels. Explain why body design matters for control, how robot design has been done with evolution, RL and differentiable simulation so far and what those approaches cannot do, and what we introduce.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Physical form affects policy optimization -> also search over the body
2. Evolutionary robot design and its limits
3. RL for robot design so far: only fixed-shape parameter changes
4. Voids/topology and our voxel-based approach
5. Why freeform design is hard; prior voxel and differentiable-simulation work
6. Our contribution: policy-gradient freeform design

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Body matters
- control policies usually optimized on a hand designed body
- physical structure can facilitate or obstruct policy optimization
- => expand search to physical parameters; structures that increasingly ease policy training

2. Evolution
- automatic robot design mainly via evolutionary algorithms (inspired by animal evolution)
- formal equivalences between learning and evolution shown
- but random phylogenetic "actions" (mutations), no bias toward beneficial mutations; same distribution start/end of evolution, not conditional on phenotype
- evolution and learning solve different kinds of problems; no RL algorithm shown capable of freeform design so far

3. RL so far
- lengthen/truncate segmented torso + pairs of jointed legs
- resize quadruped's four legs / hexapod's six
- reorganize six modular limbs during behavior
- add/remove limbs at eight predefined locations
- extrude four limbs from torso, unbalanced binary trees of depth three
- always: basic shape + internal structure predetermined; topology (number of voids) fixed

4. Voids and our approach
- voids/pores: internal carrying of objects, strength to weight ratio, surfaces for catalysis and heat exchange
- thousands of voxels as building blocks; number, placement, 3D shape of limbs and voids optimized simultaneously, minimal assumptions

5. Difficulty + prior work
- spherical particles, cubic cells used nonparametrically for geometry/topology, but not with RL
- sui generis problem: adding/reshaping/removing parts unlike resizing limbs, re-weighting synapses
- unforgiving landscape: one voxel under a bipedal walker's foot -> catastrophic behavior
- historically selection among random variations; recent sea change
- RL for 2D agents of 49 elastic voxels: unclear if geometry varied, or non-randomly; elasticity + motor layout revised, square body unchanged
- voxel-based differentiable simulation: interpolate between human-selected basis shapes, same topology for numerical stability -> trapped, topology fixed; suspended in liquid, no contact modeling -> no land-based behaviors; land offers cognitive opportunities (long-range vision and planning)
- differentiable simulation for terrestrial 2D robots extruded to 3D body plan; later extended to 3D; robot built, kept behavior; but needs custom simulation per task
- RL: only high-level reward definitions -> design machines directly

6. Contribution
- policy-gradient method for robots with freeform morphology
- any 3D shape, any internal 3D organization of materials and voids, any cartesian resolution

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Control policies are usually optimized on a robot or embodied agent whose physical form was designed by hand. But it has been shown that the physical structure of a robot can make policy optimization easier or harder. This suggests it could be useful to expand the search to also cover the physical parameters of the agent, and look for structures that make policy training easier and easier.

Inspired by how animals evolved, automatic design of robots has mostly been done with evolutionary algorithms. Formal equivalences between learning and evolution have been shown, but evolutionary robotics relies entirely on random phylogenetic “actions” (mutations) to change the design of the robot, with no bias toward favorable outcomes (beneficial mutations). In other words, mutations at the start and at the end of evolution followed the same distribution and did not depend on the state of the robot (its phenotype). Evolutionary and learning algorithms are also different in the kinds of problems they have solved successfully, and until now no reinforcement learning algorithm has been shown to be able to do freeform robot design.

Reinforcement learning (RL) and methods close to RL have been used to make a segmented torso and its pairs of jointed legs longer or shorter; to resize the four legs of a quadruped or the six legs of a hexapod; to dynamically reorganize six modular limbs during behavior; to add or remove limbs at eight predefined locations; and to extrude four limbs from a torso that branch as unbalanced binary trees of depth three. But in every one of these cases the basic geometric shape and the internal structure of the torso and limbs were fixed in advance and could not change during optimization. These algorithms also could not change the topology of the robot (number of voids).

Voids and pores could be useful for robots because they allow objects to be carried internally, they increase the strength to weight ratio of the robot, and they add surfaces for catalysis and heat exchange. Our approach uses thousands of atomic elements, voxels, as the building blocks of macrostructures, and this allows the number, placement, and 3D shape of both limbs and voids to be optimized at the same time with minimal assumptions.

5. Difficulty + prior work
- spherical particles, cubic cells used nonparametrically for geometry/topology, but not with RL
- sui generis problem: adding/reshaping/removing parts unlike resizing limbs, re-weighting synapses
- unforgiving landscape: one voxel under a bipedal walker's foot -> catastrophic behavior
- historically selection among random variations; recent sea change
- RL for 2D agents of 49 elastic voxels: unclear if geometry varied, or non-randomly; elasticity + motor layout revised, square body unchanged
- voxel-based differentiable simulation: interpolate between human-selected basis shapes, same topology for numerical stability -> trapped, topology fixed; suspended in liquid, no contact modeling -> no land-based behaviors; land offers cognitive opportunities (long-range vision and planning)
- differentiable simulation for terrestrial 2D robots extruded to 3D body plan; later extended to 3D; robot built, kept behavior; but needs custom simulation per task
- RL: only high-level reward definitions -> design machines directly

6. Contribution
- policy-gradient method for robots with freeform morphology
- any 3D shape, any internal 3D organization of materials and voids, any cartesian resolution

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Control policies are usually optimized on a robot or embodied agent whose physical form was designed by hand. But it has been shown that the physical structure of a robot can make policy optimization easier or harder. This suggests it could be useful to expand the search to also cover the physical parameters of the agent, and look for structures that make policy training easier and easier.

Inspired by how animals evolved, automatic design of robots has mostly been done with evolutionary algorithms. Formal equivalences between learning and evolution have been shown, but evolutionary robotics relies entirely on random phylogenetic “actions” (mutations) to change the design of the robot, with no bias toward favorable outcomes (beneficial mutations). In other words, mutations at the start and at the end of evolution followed the same distribution and did not depend on the state of the robot (its phenotype). Evolutionary and learning algorithms are also different in the kinds of problems they have solved successfully, and until now no reinforcement learning algorithm has been shown to be able to do freeform robot design.

Reinforcement learning (RL) and methods close to RL have been used to make a segmented torso and its pairs of jointed legs longer or shorter; to resize the four legs of a quadruped or the six legs of a hexapod; to dynamically reorganize six modular limbs during behavior; to add or remove limbs at eight predefined locations; and to extrude four limbs from a torso that branch as unbalanced binary trees of depth three. But in every one of these cases the basic geometric shape and the internal structure of the torso and limbs were fixed in advance and could not change during optimization. These algorithms also could not change the topology of the robot (number of voids).

Voids and pores could be useful for robots because they allow objects to be carried internally, they increase the strength to weight ratio of the robot, and they add surfaces for catalysis and heat exchange. Our approach uses thousands of atomic elements, voxels, as the building blocks of macrostructures, and this allows the number, placement, and 3D shape of both limbs and voids to be optimized at the same time with minimal assumptions.

Previous studies have used spherical particles and cubic cells to automatically optimize robot geometry and topology in a nonparametric way, but RL methods have not been used for this yet. Part of the reason for this gap in the literature is that the design problem is sui generis. Freely adding, reshaping and removing body parts is fundamentally different from resizing limbs and re-weighting synapses. The search landscape is much less forgiving of mistakes: for example adding or removing even one voxel on the underside of the foot of a bipedal walker could have catastrophic consequences for its behavior. Historically this meant the problem was left to selection among random variations. But in recent years there has been a sea change in robot design.

One study used RL to design 2D agents made of 49 elastic voxels. But it was not clear whether the geometry of the agent changed during training, and if it did, whether the changes were applied non-randomly. When the agent was optimized for locomotion, its elasticity and motor layout were changed, but its square body shape stayed the same.

Another study also used a voxel-based approach. Instead of RL, it used gradient information from differentiable simulation to interpolate between basis shapes selected by humans. For numerical stability, these body shapes had to share the same topology. So the learner was trapped in the design space between hand-designed shapes and could not change the topology of the robot. Also, the robots in that study were suspended in a liquid without contact modeling. Contact modeling can be hard to implement in a differentiable way, but without it land-based behaviors cannot be realized. This distinction matters for AI because land gives agents cognitive opportunities that aquatic environments do not have (e.g. long-range vision and planning).

A third study used differentiable simulation for freeform design and optimization of robots that were terrestrial but 2D. The two dimensional design space was extruded into a third dimension to give a physical 3D body plan. More recently, others have extended differentiable design to three dimensions. The robot from that study was built and was found to keep its behavior, but it is not clear how methods relying on differentiable physics can work without a custom built simulation for every new task the robot faces. RL on the other hand only needs high-level reward definitions, so it can design physical machines directly without recourse to simulations.

So here we introduce a policy-gradient method for designing robots with freeform morphology. The robots are freeform in the sense that they can be generated with any 3D shape and any internal 3D organization of materials and voids, at any given cartesian resolution.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Control policies are usually optimized on a robot or embodied agent with a hand designed physical form. However, it has been shown that a robot's physical structure can facilitate or obstruct policy optimization [1,2,3,4]. This suggests that it may be useful to expand the search to encompass the physical parameters of an agent as well, looking for structures that increasingly ease policy training.

Inspired by the evolution of animals, the automatic design of robots has mainly been achieved using evolutionary algorithms [5,6,7,2,8,3,4]. Although formal equivalences have been shown between learning and evolution [9], evolutionary robotics relies entirely on random phylogenetic “actions” (mutations) to modify the robot's design, with no bias toward favorable outcomes (beneficial mutations). That is, mutations at the beginning and at the end of evolution followed the same distribution and were not conditional on the state of the robot (its phenotype). Evolutionary and learning algorithms also differ in the kinds of problems they have successfully solved, and until now no reinforcement learning algorithm has been shown to be capable of freeform robot design.

Reinforcement learning (RL) and RL-adjacent methods have been used to lengthen or truncate a segmented torso and its pairs of jointed legs [10]; to resize a quadruped's four legs [11,12,13] or a hexapod's six [14]; to dynamically reorganize six modular limbs during behavior [15]; to add or remove limbs at eight predefined locations [16]; and to extrude four limbs from a torso that branch as unbalanced binary trees of depth three [17]. But in every case, the basic geometric shape and internal structure of the robot's torso and limbs were predetermined and could not change during optimization. Nor could these algorithms alter the robot's topology (number of voids).

Voids and pores could be useful for robots since they allow objects to be carried internally, increase the robot's strength to weight ratio, and add surfaces for catalysis and heat exchange. Our approach uses thousands of atomic elements (voxels) as the building blocks of macrostructures, which allows the number, placement, and 3D shape of limbs and voids to be optimized simultaneously, with minimal assumptions.

Spherical particles [18] and cubic cells [19] have been used in previous studies to automatically optimize robot geometry and topology in a nonparametric manner, but RL methods have yet to leverage them for this purpose. This gap in the literature is partly due to the sui generis nature of the design problem. Freely adding, reshaping and removing body parts is fundamentally different from resizing limbs and re-weighting synapses. The search landscape is much less forgiving of missteps: adding or removing even a single voxel along the underside of a bipedal walker's foot, for instance, could have catastrophic behavioral consequences. Historically, this relegated the problem to selection among random variations. But recent years have seen a sea change in robot design.

[20] used RL to design 2D agents composed of 49 elastic voxels. However, it was unclear whether the agent's geometry varied during training and, if it did, whether revisions were applied non-randomly. When the agent was optimized for locomotion, its elasticity and motor layout were revised, but its square body shape remained unchanged.

[21] also took a voxel-based approach, but instead of RL, used gradient information from differentiable simulation to interpolate between human-selected basis shapes. To ensure numerical stability, these body shapes had to share the same topology, so the learner was trapped in the design space between hand-designed shapes and could not alter the robot's topology. Also, the robots in [21] were suspended in a liquid without contact modeling, which can be challenging to implement in a differentiable fashion and without which land-based behaviors cannot be realized. This is an important distinction for AI, as land affords agents cognitive opportunities that are absent in aquatic environments (e.g. long-range vision and planning [22]).

[23] used differentiable simulation for the freeform design and optimization of terrestrial yet 2D robots, extruding the two dimensional design space into a third dimension to yield a physical 3D body plan. More recently, others [24,25] have extended differentiable design to three dimensions. While the robot from [23] was built and found to retain its behavior, it is unclear how methods relying on differentiable physics can proceed without a custom built simulation for every new task the robot faces. RL, in contrast, requires only high-level reward definitions and can therefore design physical machines directly without recourse to simulations.

We therefore introduce a policy-gradient method for designing robots with freeform morphology. The resulting robots are freeform in the sense that they can be generated with any 3D shape and any internal 3D organization of materials and voids, at any given cartesian resolution.
